description.contents: The course has three components, each with a different focus:Lectures focus on the social history of the English language from its roots to Early Modern English. We will start from before English to the arrival of English in England and its interactions with the native Celtic population, Christianization, the Viking and Norman invasions, and Caxton and the printing press, among many other topics. Not only are important events and their social impact covered but also their influences on the development of the language, in particular its rich vocabulary, including inherited words, various word formation processes, and borrowings.Linguistics seminars cover the concepts and terminology of morphology and applying these in basic morphological analyses of sets of data, including texts from the Old, Middle and Early Modern English periods.Academic skills seminars focus on reading and understanding academic research, summarizing and paraphrasing for academic purposes, APA referencing style, and synthesizing sources in academic writing.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to:identify and discuss key socio-historical and political events and circumstances in the history of English that have had an impact on its development, in particular on its vocabulary;demonstrate knowledge of basic concepts and terminology of morphology;carry out basic morphological analyses on (novel) sets of data;write a short, cohesive, thesis-driven paper drawing on an academic source to support the argument.
description.entryRequirements: This course is intended for first-year BA students of English Language and Culture. Other students interested in taking the course must contact the course coordinator to determine whether their level of English is high enough and whether there is enough space.

uva-elc-y1-lit1.name: English Literature 1: Genres, Texts and Contexts

description.contents: This 6EC course introduces students to foundational practical and critical skills required for academic literary studies. Working with sets of specific literary terms and concepts, students develop the ability to produce confident evaluations in effective argumentative essays in relation to specific literary genres, including lyrical poetry, short stories, novellas, novels and drama. With a focus on practical criticism and close-reading strategies, students are also introduced to relevant intellectual literary traditions and historical contexts, as well as familiarized with fundamental topics and academic terminology in the field of literary studies. In so doing, this course lays the groundwork for subsequent literary courses by advancing critical reading, interpretative and analytical skills. The course is taught by means of weekly lectures, literature seminars, and academic skills seminars. The academic skills seminars focus on developing students’ writing and research skills that will support their literary work throughout the BA English Language and Culture program.
description.objectives: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:read and respond in an informed manner to literary texts from different periods by establishing connections and disjunctions across selected genres, and take an evaluative position on literary inheritance, influence and transmission; demonstrate close-reading abilities, sensitivity to literary language and formal features at a level appropriate to undergraduate literary study by working with relevant critical and literary terms;research and write a literary academic essay while incorporating academic criticism and/or historical material with clear, appropriately structured with well-developed arguments whilst being cognizant of academic conventions;demonstrate a basic knowledge of academic skills including MLA citation style, essay structure, and tools for conducting academic research.

description.contents: The course focuses on the spread of English across the world and the diversity that this brings about. We adopt the World Englishes perspective and trace the spread of English through colonial expansion to North America, the Caribbean, Africa, Asia and Australasia, before considering the consequences of modern-day globalisation and its reinforcement of the global role of English. Major types of linguistic consequences, resulting from language contact and contact between people in new environments, are considered, with a particular emphasis on variation in the pronunciation of English world-wide. Basic concepts from phonology are introduced to support the analysis of variation in English pronunciation. Academic English skills are developed in the context of academic essay writing, with attention to the appropriate development of an argument and the incorporation of linguistic material as data.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:describe the extent of, explain the reasons for, and identify the most important linguistic consequences of, the spread of English around the world;apply basic phonological concepts to analyse selected phonological characteristics of varieties of English;compose concise arguments based on scholarly discourse and key concepts in World Englishes;present a review of selected case studies of English varieties based on academic sources, applying at least one model of the spread of English to the relevant varieties;write an academic essay on a topic in World Englishes, using the appropriate rhetorical features, integrating relevant sources, reporting linguistic data concisely and accurately, and presenting an argument with adequate justification.
description.entryRequirements: This course is intended for first-year BA students of English Language and Culture. Other students interested in taking the course must contact the course coordinator to determine whether their level of English is high enough and whether there is enough space.

description.contents: Each week, the course will explore one of the major bodies of literary theory, such as Marxism, feminism, postcolonialism, psychoanalysis, and poststructuralism. Lectures will focus on presenting conceptual material, while seminars will develop the skill of "applying" these theories to literary texts. The combination of English Literature 1 and Literary Theory provides students with the foundation of theoretical awareness and close reading skill that will inform and be further developed by their other literary studies throughout the English degree.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:define and understand various critical and theoretical concepts;recognize and engage critically in both writing and speech with theoretical approaches used in literary criticism;develop readings of literary texts that draw on theory;adapt theoretical approaches for use in their own scholarly writing;demonstrate noticeable improvements in their academic writing and close reading/analytical skills.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Students should have done English Literature 1: Genres, Texts and Contexts before this course.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This course is introductory. The only recommended prior knowledge is a grasp of the rudiments of close reading, which are imparted in English Literature 1.

description.contents: In this course you will investigate the cultural, critical and historical significance of the novel Frankenstein (1818/30) by Mary Shelley. Two seminars in the first two weeks of the course will explore different approaches and critical perspectives towards the text. You will then undertake an independent research project leading to a class conference day in week four, where you will present your research orally in a ten-minute paper to the rest of the group. The third week of the course will include a peer-review session where students discuss their conference paper proposals with their peers. During the conference day, students will be invited to respond to one another's presentations and ask questions. The course is designed to provide a chance for intensive research into a single significant work of English literature, building on English Literature 1 (which you will normally have taken in a previous block) and preparing you for future literary research, including the BA thesis.
description.objectives: During this course you will:gain an in-depth understanding of a particular novel (Frankenstein) which is of significant cultural and critical significance;build on skills learnt in English Literature 1 to undertake an independent research project into a specific aspect of the text in focus;produce an appropriate research plan for your project;present your research to peers and the seminar tutor as part of a class conference day;engage with and respond to fellow students' presentations during the conference day.
description.entryRequirements: Previous participation in English Literature 1: Genres, Texts and Contexts is a pre-requisite for this course.

description.contents: This course provides students with a rich knowledge of significant literary works from the Early Modern period, and it explores the intellectual, socio-cultural, and political developments that form the respective contexts of those works. Course readings include poetry, drama, and prose from the Renaissance and the Restoration. The authors we will study include William Shakespeare, Mary Wroth, John Donne, John Milton, and Aphra Behn. In Literature 2, we consider the continuities as much as the differences between texts as we situate works in their immediate context. Students will hone the critical abilities that they developed in Literature 1 as they further develop and strengthen their capacities as interpreters of, and respondents to, English literature.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, you will: be able to analyse and discuss diverse forms of literature from the period 1550-1700;be able both to recognize and discuss characteristics of literature from each period under analysis, and to reflect upon connections between works of literature across time;understand key elements of the development of English literature, including the sonnet, epic poetry, and drama, and the role of socio-historical context in that development;be able to identify and critically assess pertinent evidence to develop a cogent argument.

description.contents: This course aims to enrich your written and spoken English at an advanced academic level. The course will focus on three main areas: rhetoric, creative writing and vocabulary building. The study of rhetoric will show you that rhetoric, far from being an antiquated discipline, is all around us. It determines the nature of most of the spoken and written language we hear and see around us, as well as that which we produce. Rhetoric is what underlies good argumentation and persuasion, essential skills for a student of English. As such, the knowledge gained during this course will be useful throughout the rest of the BA programme, no matter whether your personal interests lie in language or in literature. You will analyze a wide range of influential speeches, learning to recognize the persuasive techniques at work on a language level. You will put your newly acquired knowledge into practice by delivering your own in-class speech. The classes also focus on literary style and creative writing as a means of developing and improving your own writing skills. You will study, analyze and imitate various literary styles in order to improve your own writing style.
description.objectives: At the end of the course, you will:have acquired a basic knowledge of the theory and history of rhetoric;be able to use your knowledge of rhetoric to analyse political speeches;have learned how to write persuasive speeches;be able to analyse various literary styles using basic syntactic (grammatical) tools;be able to imitate various literary styles;have increased your vocabulary to an advanced academic level.

description.contents: The main aim of this course will be to equip you with the tools and knowledge necessary to analyse English sentences. We will start by learning about the main concepts and theories pertaining to the grammatical analysis of sentences, drawing on both formal and functional approaches. We will then focus on specific levels in the structure. You will thus learn how to recognise, describe and analyse English sentences, both in isolation and within a broader context. Finally, we will apply this knowledge to learning how to analyse the variation in English we experience in the world today.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, you will:understand concepts related to describing the structure of English phrases, clauses and texts;be able to apply this understanding to the analyses of naturally occurring English language structures;be acquainted with different approaches to the study of English syntactic structures;have learned how to describe the structural variation that can be observed in World Englishes;have gained academic writing skills, such as summarising, paraphrasing and critically evaluating sources, as well as reporting on research and describing research results.
description.entryRequirements: This course is intended for first-year BA students of English Language and Culture. For other students admission to the course is only possible if there are places available after the regular students have been placed.

description.contents: The eighteenth century saw the unification of Britain and the nation’s global expansion through trade and colonialism, the development of commercial public spaces, and the emergence of the novel as a dominant form of literature in English.This course provides a roughly chronological overview of literature in English from the period, focusing on the development of various genres in this period such as the novel and the essay. Along with (excerpts from) canonical works of prose fiction such as Eliza Haywood's Fantomina, Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels, and Frances Burney's Evelina, we will read a range of poems from the period, including those by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and excerpts from social, scientific and philosophical texts including Olaudah Equiano's Interesting Narrative, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu’s Turkish Embassy Letters, and Addison Spectator papers. The seminars that follow each of the weekly lectures will provide students with an opportunity to discuss course texts in greater depth, developing skills in close analysis and comparison, and in relation to major social issues, such as class conflict, slavery and abolition, and gender roles.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to:analyse and discuss diverse forms of literature from the 18th century;identify key social and historical changes that took place in the 18th century;understand and identify the aesthetic characteristics of the various literary texts under study;employ terms related to the literary history of the 18th century, such as ‘satire’ and ‘the sublime’;construct a reasoned argument about primary texts from the period, supported by appropriate use of evidence and close analysis.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This course builds on some of the material covered on English Literature 1 and 2, but participation in Literature 2 is not a requirement for students from outside the BA English Language and Culture.

uva-elc-y1-ling4.name: English Linguistics 4: Research in English Linguistics

description.contents: The goal of this course is to familiarise students with a range of basic concepts and methods in linguistic research. The course covers a range of theoretical and practical issues in language research relating to the different data types and methodologies that will be covered in the course (e.g. interviews, questionnaires, experiments, corpora). In addition, different types of data will be approached practically, allowing the students to develop basic data-analytic skills. The course consists of two complementary parts: (1) a lecture component and (2) a seminar component. The lectures will provide you with a concise introduction to the key concepts in empirical research. In the seminars you will be applying this knowledge in practical exercises on the topic of a given week.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of the course, you will have developed the skills to:read, work with, analyze, and argue with data (data literacy);understand important principles of research design and commonly used methodologies in linguistic research;critically evaluate qualitative and quantitative analyses of published research in the language sciences.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: 18 EC, which must include English Linguistics 1: Stories of English ; English Linguistics 2: English and Englishes , English Linguistics 3: Language in Use , or equivalent courses elsewhere.

description.contents: This course provides an overview of English Literature in the nineteenth century, focusing on Romantic and Victorian Britain. The course explores the changing relationship between individual and society during this period, and traces the development of some of its most significant debates, movements and genres. We begin by considering how early-nineteenth-century writers developed new responses to questions about nature, self and society that had become increasingly pressing in the aftermath of 1789. This sets the stage for reading literature as an inherently social and political exercise, engaged with concerns around class, urbanisation, empire, race, evolution and gender roles, among other topics. We will also examine how literature increasingly came to dwell on the modern psyche, by exploring its interest in moral and psychological degeneration, and in the relationship between madness and representation.Alongside major literary works such as Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Eyre (1847) and Jekyll and Hyde (1886), we will read excerpts from social, scientific and philosophical texts such as Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859). Seminars build on weekly lectures by providing the opportunity to discuss course texts in relation to social issues, and introduce students to important critical and theoretical approaches to the period.
description.objectives: On successful completion of this course you will be able to:identify key social and historical changes of the nineteenth century in Britain and beyond;understand and identify the aesthetic characteristics of the various literary movements under study;employ terms related to the literary history of the nineteenth century, such as ‘romanticism’, ‘realism’ and ‘Gothic’;employ close reading skills to analyse the texts on the course, in the light of broad themes and patterns of development that bear upon them.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: You are expected to have begun to study English Literature or a closely related subject at university level, and to be familiar with the core expectations of the discipline.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: You are recommended to have taken English Literature 3: The Eighteenth Century before joining this course, or to otherwise have a basic understanding of English Literature before the nineteenth century. You are also expected to have some experience of writing essays on literary topics.

uva-elc-y2-lit5.name: English Literature 5: Modern and Contemporary Literature

description.contents: This course will provide an overview of modernism and postmodernism using key texts in order to analyse the development of literature and literary theory in the 20th century, in particular those writers and thinkers who attempted to break with received norms of literary style and content. Each text will be read in its most integrative context, taking into consideration the cultural and artistic pressures that surround its development, including: historical factors (such as war, the modern metropolis, technological industrialization), the shifting nature of identity and selfhood (including the roles of race, gender and class), and the critical contexts that influenced both literary production and reception (such as New Criticism and Poststructuralism), thereby exploring critical attempts to define these movements and to comprehend their aims. Finally, by recognizing co-incidental movements, the survey will cover the modernist shift away from earlier literary forms (especially realism), the subsequent emergence of the postmodern impulse, and how those two legacies have been negotiated in more recent texts.
description.objectives: Students who successfully complete the course will:have grasped the various theories behind modernism, postmodernism and other relevant C20th isms, and to have understood both the aesthetic characteristics and intellectual and social contexts of each movement;demonstrate an advanced ability to interrelate texts (in the genres of the novel, drama and poetry) and discourses specific to modernism and postmodernism to issues in wider context of social and cultural history;learn how to assess the critical reception of a literary work and evaluate different approaches;demonstrate effective communication, analytical, and research skills, both individually – in the essay through the construction of a coherent, substantiated argument, in clear and correct prose – and in groups, by means of oral presentations.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Students ought to have completed English Literature 1: Genres, Texts and Contexts, English Literature 2: Early Modern Literature, English Literature 3: The Eighteenth Century and English Literature 4: The Nineteenth Century.

description.contents: In this course you will investigate the cultural, critical and historical significance of one important literary text from the twentieth or twenty-first century, chosen by the seminar tutor. Two seminars in the first two weeks of the course will explore different approaches and critical perspectives towards the text. You will then undertake an independent research project leading to a class conference day, where you will present your research orally in a ten-minute paper to the rest of the group. The third week of the course will include a peer-review session where students discuss their conference paper proposals with their peers. During the conference day, students will be invited to respond to one another's presentations and ask questions. The course is designed to provide a chance for intensive research into a single significant work of English literature, building on English Literature 5 (which students will have taken in the previous block).
description.objectives: Students who successfully complete the course will:gain an in-depth understanding of a particular novel or other literary text (the 'text in focus') which is of significant cultural or critical significance;demonstrate an advanced ability to place the text under study in the wider context of cultural and intellectual history;understand the essential literary skills and critical methodologies which can usefully be applied to the 'text in focus';demonstrate appropriate research and bibliographic skills and an advanced capacity to construct a coherent, substantiated argument;demonstrate effective oral communication skills, and an ability to work well individually.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities. Students must have attempted English Literature 5: Modern and Contemporary Literature in order to take this course.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Previous participation in English Literature 5: Modern and Contemporary Literature is a pre-requisite for this course.

description.contents: In this introductory course to sociolinguistics, we will address the fundamental issues of the positioning of language in human societies and the ways in which language functions in interaction. While keeping varieties of English as a focus, our investigation will also draw from multilingual and non-English scenarios, critically examining classic sociolinguistic accounts from a contemporary perspective and recent state-of-the-art studies. This will allow you to build a solid and comprehensive understanding of the workings of language in society, as well as of the key theoretical and methodological notions of the field of sociolinguistics. Topics will include language variation and change, dialectology, language and gender, language and social identity, and language and culture. In terms of methodologies, you will gain practical knowledge of a range of core sociolinguistic methods and will learn how to use sociolinguistic interviews, questionnaires, and (social media) corpora in the context of conducting original sociolinguistic research.
description.objectives: At the end of the course, you will be able to:explain and exemplify key concepts and theories in the field of sociolinguistics;understand and describe a range of methodological approaches in the field of sociolinguistics;solve specific theoretical and/or methodological problems related to language in society;apply theoretical and methodological knowledge to the analysis of sociolinguistic data;carry out an original sociolinguistic study, using appropriate methodology;communicate your research findings in a paper and a presentation.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for English Language and Culture.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Students taking this course are assumed to have good knowledge of basic notions from English phonetics/phonology, morphology and syntax, as acquired through the following courses from the English Language and Culture BA programme:English Linguistics 1: Stories of EnglishEnglish Linguistics 2: English and EnglishesEnglish Linguistics 3: Language in UseStudents who have not followed these courses should have ideally obtained this knowledge in other ways (e.g. other courses/other universities/introductory textbooks in the areas mentioned).
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: It is recommended – but not required – that students have some basic knowledge of research methods and basic data literacy skills, as acquired through the following course from the English Language and Culture BA programme or equivalent:English Linguistics 4: Research in English Linguistics

uva-elc-y2-ling6.name: English Linguistics 6: The Changing English Language

description.contents: In this course, we cover language change processes in English in terms of language-internal mechanisms. Building on the knowledge from the linguistics courses in Year 1, we cover the principles and rules that govern changes in the structure of English sounds, words and sentences. We explore the fundamental principles and methods of historical linguistics, which allow us to explore how language changes over time, sometimes radically, even catastrophically, while other times so gradually that speakers of the language are unaware that change is taking place at all. These processes of change can be observed and investigated in a variety of ways. We will be looking at change currently in progress as well as at changes that took place in the history of English. We will apply this knowledge to the analysis of cases of language change and focus on communicating these insights to an academic audience.
description.objectives: At the end of the course, you will be able to:explain and discuss different types of internal language change processes;define and describe the terminology, concerns and theories of various key areas in the study of language change;identify cases of language change in English and describe them in terms of language-internal mechanisms;apply this knowledge to the analysis of novel linguistic data;summarise and report in writing the results of data-based linguistic analyses, anddescribe, critically discuss and evaluate competing accounts of language change, focusing either on individual linguistic features or on more general theories.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities with some coursework in linguistics or permission from the course coordinator.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: If you have not taken the courses listed under "Recommended prior knowledge", be sure to review basic linguistic concepts and terminology from the areas of phonetics/phonology, morphology, and syntax as well as basic grammatical terminology. An introductory linguistics course or textbook should be sufficient.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: English Linguistics 1: Stories of EnglishEnglish Linguistics 2: English and EnglishesEnglish Linguistics 3: Language in UseEnglish Linguistics 5: Language in Society

uva-elc-y3-philosophy.name: Philosophy of the Humanities (LCA and English)

description.contents: The course addresses fundamental epistemological questions (what is knowledge? who is the subject of knowledge? is knowledge dependent on political or historical contexts?) by relating these to a series of contemporary philosophical ideas and theoretical concepts such as: truth and interpretation (how can we solve the tension between objective and subjective knowledge); language and identity/body (how do we understand and speak about ourselves and others?); technology and the post-human (what would the ‘post-humanities’ look like?); environment and the Anthropocene (what does climate change do to our conceptions of ‘culture’, ‘nature’ and ‘matter’?); biopolitics (how is life managed and subject to political control?); critique (what is the legacy and broader reception of critical thinking and ‘theory’?). In broad terms, we will reflect on the place of the humanities in all this. What are the humanities as a discipline? What if the ‘human sciences’ are themselves a cultural and historical phenomenon, not unlike ‘science’ and ‘the human’?
description.objectives: The general aim of this course is to provide students with a philosophical reflection on what scientific knowledge in the humanities is and how it is produced. By the end of the course, students will be familiar with key theories and paradigm shifts in the history of Western philosophy. This course will develop students' analytical thinking through engagement with theory and case studies.Name and define important traditions and frameworks in the philosophy of humanities;Explain philosophical issues as they emerge in humanities research (that are part of a text/object of analysis);Discuss and reflect in both writing and speech on the relevance of philosophical literature in our present.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities

description.contents: The Linguistics module explores some of the key debates that have taken place within linguistics over the past century. Central to these debates are the questions: (1) How far does language determine our world view, if at all? (2) Is there such a thing as Universal Grammar, i.e. are human beings endowed with innate linguistic abilities? Or does language emerge from social interaction and our general cognitive abilities? In considering these questions we will focus on English linguistics, but, for perspective, also zoom out to other languages, and to the neighbouring disciplines of philosophy and psychology.The Literature module of Debates in English Studies further develops the knowledge of critical approaches and theoretical concepts first introduced in Literary Theory. Unlike that course, this course will not involve “applied” sessions in which literary texts are interpreted. Rather, it will focus on the theoretical texts themselves. In addition to enhancing students’ general knowledge of theory, this course as a whole aims to improve students’ ability to engage with theoretically-abstract texts. In short, Debates in English Studies develops students’ competence and confidence in grappling independently with key ideas that emerge from the nexus of literary theory and philosophy.
description.objectives: Depending on the orientation of their BA thesis projects, students will choose to participate in either the linguistics or the literature seminar of this course. (The lingustics seminiars will cover bullet points 1-4; the literature seminars will cover bullet points 5-8.)Upon successful completion of the course, you will: be familiar with some of the most persistent debates within (English) linguistics over the past century;understand the opposing sides of these debates, and the middle ground;understand the relevance of other languages and other disciplines to debates within lingusitics;be able to explain the issues to a layperson as well as to your peers;define, understand and intervene in a variety of theoretical debates within literary criticism;debate how the socially-constructed dimension of language, meaning, representation, and communication informs various literary theories;understand how various theoretical approaches supplement and complement one another within literary criticism;adapt theoretical approaches for use in your own scholarly writing.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Linguistics: students are expected to be have completed all first-year English Linguistics courses, namely: English Linguistics 1: Stories of English, English Linguistics 2: English and Englishes, English Linguistics 3: Language in Use, English Linguistics 4: Research in English Linguistics.Literature: students are expected to be familiar with the material covered in Literary Theory.

description.contents: Depending on the orientation of their BA thesis projects, students will choose to participate in either the linguistics or the literature seminar of this course.The module revisits some key aspects of research in linguistics and literature, including research methodologies, and pertinent theories and debates. Through plenary discussions, peer review, and preparatory research in the form of an annotated bibliography, and a draft chapter, students will begin writing sections of their thesis at an early stage in the course.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of the course, you will have developed the skills to:formulate, research, and present your chosen thesis topic;demonstrate the research and writing skills needed for successful completion of a BA thesis in Literature or Linguistics;produce a significant body of work that will contribute to the final BA thesis.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for English Language and Culture and students must have passed all compulsory English courses in year 1 and 2. Exception is possible for students who have yet to follow English Literature 5: Modern and Contemporary Literature. Students must enter the course with a research topic that can be investigated from the outset.

uva-elc-y3-thesis.name: Bachelor's Thesis English Language and Culture

description.contents: Detailed information about the course is provided in the BA Thesis Regulations, located on the Canvas page for the BA Thesis.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to:make independent use of the knowledge, methodologies and skills you have been taught over the course of the programme;produce an extended written thesis that is appropriately structured, addressing an independently defined and well-focused subject related to English Literature or English Language/Linguistics;conduct guided independent academic research to contextualise and inform your thesis;work with a supervisor to revise and develop your project over the course of the supervision period.
description.entryRequirements: At least 108 ECTs of the Bachelor programme must be completed before students begin writing their theses. The 108 ECTs to be completed prior to beginning the thesis should include all the core courses for the BA degree in English Language and Culture. Students following the English Language and Culture programme will receive general guidance in the thesis writing process by following a course specifically designed for that purpose, entitled English Research Seminar. If students fail the Research Seminar, they may not complete their BA thesis until the following academic year.

description.contents: Academic literacy skills are essential to successfully completing your Bachelor's degree. Throughout your studies, you will be expected to read and understand increasingly complex academic texts, consider the nuance of specific words or sentences, and write your own essays and papers where you show your ability to evaluate and reflect on complex matter. To help you with this, all first-year BA students at the Faculty of Humanities take the Academic Literacy Test in September so that extra academic writing support can be provided to those who need it. The aim of the test is to give you insight into your academic literacy skills and which areas you may still need to work on in order to do well in your studies. If you fail the test, you will be enrolled for an extracurricular Academic Writing Support course, which provides extra support and individual feedback aimed at helping you do well you in the rest of your studies.Please note that this is not a language test, such as TOEFL or IELTS. It is designed to make sure both native and non-native speakers of English get the support and guidance they need.
description.objectives: The purpose of the Academic Literacy Test is to:gauge the level of your academic literacy skills, such as reading, reasoning and writing;provide you with extra support in these areas if necessary.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Since this is a diagnostic test, there is no need to prepare or study for it.

58253.name: Tutoring and Study Guidance Bachelor's in English Language and Culture

description.contents: At the beginning of each academic year, you will be assigned a lecturer as your tutor, with whom you can discuss your study progress in an individual meeting. Your tutor might also organise group meetings about relevant topics. This will enable you to keep track of the content and structure of your programme and plan accordingly.Your tutor is your first point of contact for questions regarding curricular aspects of your programme. A tutor's role is different from that of a study adviser or student psychologist in that he or she is a lecturer with knowledge of the course content. Another important aspect of the tutor’s role is to refer you to the study adviser.
description.objectives: The purposes of tutoring are: To reflect with your tutor on your study performance, choices and progress within your degree programme.To familiarise you with the rules and customs of an academic degree programme and to facilitate your integration into the programme and the University.

approvedElectiveExamples.name: Language in Literature: a Stylistic Approach

description.contents: This course connects linguistics with literature by examining the relationship between (linguistic) form and meaning. This approach to literature – known as stylistics – explores how authors play with language in order to create meaning, and how readers respond to language and infer meaning. Being able to recognise and analyse how language works in literature is essential for students of both literature and linguistics, and particularly inspiring for students who are interested in creative writing. In short, this course will equip you with a stylistic toolkit that will not only enrich your personal response to literary works but also improve your critical reading skills and stimulate your creative writing skills.
description.objectives: Having successfully completed the course, you will be able to:recognize and analyse the stylistic choices made by an author;recognize and analyse how these stylistic choices contribute to a text’s meaning;use stylistic terminology to carry out a stylistic analysis;use your knowledge of stylistics to hone your critical reading skills.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for English Language and Culture.

approvedElectiveExamples.name: Charles Dickens and the Making of the Modern World

description.contents: More than any other writer, Charles Dickens has come to represent the Victorian era for contemporary readers, but his works are richer and more complex than popular images of ragged orphans and cruel misers might suggest. On this course you will develop a detailed understanding of Dickens’s writing by engaging with a broad range of his writings, from the journalistic writing of the 1830s to the social tapestries of the 1850s. We will look in detail at two major novels: Oliver Twist and Bleak House, as well as a selection of shorter texts, such as A Christmas Carol, in order to consider Dickens’s engagement with the major issues of his day, including poverty and wealth, the modern city, law and criminality, financial speculation, gender roles, madness, empire, and the growth of capitalism. We will also look at various critical contexts for Dickens's work, and at adaptation via Armando Iannucci's The Personal History of David Copperfield (2019). The course ends by considering Hannah Crafts's rewriting of Bleak House in the context of American slavery in The Bondwoman's Narrative (1853-61?).
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of the course you will be able to:demonstrate a good understanding of Dickens’s literary career and its social and historical contexts;identify and critically assess pertinent evidence to develop a cogent argument;employ close reading skills effectively in relation to the primary texts;identify and analyse themes and patterns of development in the texts under consideration;show an understanding of and make evaluations of some major critical approaches to the primary texts;demonstrate a critical understanding of key contexts of the period, such as crime, poverty and wealth, modernity, gender roles and empire.
description.entryRequirements: A positive binding study advice (BSA) for a Bachelor in Humanities.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Students are expected to have studied English Literature at university level and to be familiar with the expectations of the discipline.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: It is recommended that students are familiar with the history, culture and literature of nineteenth-century Britain (for instance, from taking English Literature 4: The Nineteenth Century).

progression: First year has 30 EC per semester. The academic literacy test and tutoring carry zero credits. Passing all 60 EC meets the faculty 48 EC full-time positive study advice requirement and supplies the English linguistics and literature background.

Year two first semester uses English Literature 4, Language in Society and 12 EC of free electives. The second semester uses Changing English Language, English Literature 5 and Texts in Focus 2, plus 12 EC programme-related electives. Stylistics and the Dickens course illustrate feasible approved options in periods 4 and 5 without narrowing the displayed elective pool. English Literature 5 precedes Texts in Focus 2.

Year three starts with philosophy, debates, research seminar and part of the 30 EC free choice. The research seminar requires positive study advice and the compulsory English courses from years one and two, with a limited exception for Literature 5. The thesis is in periods 5 and 6, requires 108 EC and all core courses, and depends on passing the research seminar. Completing the first two years gives 120 EC and the route completes the seminar before writing.
